newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: East European states count cost of NATO decision.
newsitem.headline: East European states count cost of NATO decision.

text.p: Central and East European leaders on Thursday assessed the fall-out from NATO's decision to invite three of their number to join the alliance, drawing a fresh dividing line across the region.
Politicians from the successful candidates -- the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary -- had fulsome praise for the decision, taken at NATO's Madrid summit earlier this week.
Countries that failed to make the grade swallowed their disappointment, pinning their hopes on NATO's promise that its door remained open to potential new members.

"If we do this right everybody will see himself as a winner of the (Madrid) summit. If not we will have failed," Robert Hunter, U.S. ambassador to NATO in Brussels, told delegates at the second Central and East European Summit in Salzburg.
The alliance is due for another membership review in 1999, the year the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary will join.
"I must say that NATO in 1999 is quite acceptable," Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek told a news conference.
Slovenia, like Romania, failed by a hair's breadth to win NATO entry this time round.
Unanimous in their gratitude to NATO for inviting them in, the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary were also unanimously vague on the potential costs and benefits of membership.
"This invitation probably does ratchet up our standing among foreign investors," said Karel Kovanda, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs from the Czech Republic.
"(But) we do not know how to quantify what it is going to cost us to join NATO, never mind quantify the benefits," he added.
Kovanda also sought to play down talk of a new order of "haves" and "have nots" in Eastern Europe, less than a decade after the iron curtain fell.
"While (NATO membership) may help us...I would not see the resulting differences quite as dramatic as to constitute a new dividing line," he said.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Marek Belka said his country's military budget would easily be able to absorb NATO-related charges, which he estimated at $100 to $200 million annually, spread out over several years.
"Of course, there are some immediate costs connected with NATO membership...but this is not huge. This is something that can be borne by the military budget alone easily," he said.

Most of the money would go into upgrading telecommunications and command systems to make them compatible with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's standards, added Belka, who is also finance minister.

Russia staunchly opposed any inclusion of former communist countries in NATO. Yevgeny Yasin, minister without portfolio in the Moscow cabinet, said Moscow wanted to ensure the alliance's expansion did not bring any negative results.
"We will continue our policy of cooperation with Western countries and our partners in Eastern Europe," he said.
Yasin told Reuters he did not expect NATO's decision to harm foreign investment in Russia. "Potential investors are looking at other factors," he said.
